title: Olive and Dotty's Wreath Adventure
markdown:
Once upon a time, in a meadow the sun liked to kiss, an otter named Olive and a dachshund named Dotty shared a stream. Olive’s whiskers twitched like tiny antennae. She loved the next bend, and the slide of mossy rock under her sleek brown fur. Dotty’s tail wiggled as if it had borrowed a hundred fireflies. She loved the sweetest-smelling flowers along the bank, and she loved Olive just as much.

Every day they played the same gentle game. Olive glided from rock to rock in the shallow water, a whisper of brown against the sparkle. The stream sang over pebbles. Dotty chased butterfly-shadows on the grass. Sometimes a brave butterfly landed on her nose, and she froze, tail giving one curious twitch, until the butterfly thought better of it and lifted away. Olive would laugh a little otter-laugh, and they would start again.

Until one day the Muffins moved in. They were a family of field mice with tiny round ears, and they were famous for the tiniest, roundest muffins. Their new burrow sat near the stream, and the entrance looked bare, like a doorway that had forgotten to put on its coat.

Olive wriggled her nose. “Oh, Dotty. It needs a hug of welcoming. A warm fuzzy blanket for their door.”

“A wreath,” Dotty declared, ears perking, tail going thump-thump-thump on the dew. “Pretty leaves. So they know they’re home.”

Because of that they launched a leaf-collecting adventure. Their boat was a little log, hollowed by time and smooth as a river stone. It bobbed in the shallows. Olive steered with gentle paw-nudges. Dotty was chief leaf-spotter, nose twitching for colour.

The water chuckled around them. Willow light dappled their fur gold. Olive spotted a leaf the colour of a ripe strawberry, heart-shaped and perfect.

“This one,” she squeaked. “A tiny valentine.”

Dotty nudged a leaf that shone like a new coin. “Extra shiny. Sunshine trapped inside.”

They gathered more: emerald velvet, melted butter, sunset blush. The stream was shallow enough that their paws could touch sand when they needed to steady the boat. Olive dipped her paws and paddled. Dotty leaned over, sniffing, once nearly tipping them for a leaf that turned out to be only a yellow pebble. She woofed at herself, and Olive steered them straight again.

Because of that they followed the curve past a patch of wild roses. There, on a low branch, hung leaves they had never seen. Olive stopped paddling. The log drifted. A bee went by, uninterested in silver. The leaves shimmered, cool and smooth as a sliver of moon. A faint honeysuckle smell came off them. Each leaf held a tiny twinkling of cloud, like a window the size of a thumbnail. They rustled like tiny sighs.

Olive and Dotty sat in the log and looked. They did not grab at once. Water tapped the wood. A rose petal fell and floated away like a small boat of its own. The strawberry-heart leaf in their pile felt familiar and warm. The butter-yellow one was captured sun. The silver ones were something else.

“They feel like starlight,” Olive whispered.

Dotty’s tail went still, which for Dotty was a kind of bow.

Until finally Olive steered close. Dotty used her nose, very gently, to nudge the shimmering leaves aboard. The log sat lower in the water, brimming. They paddled home with the sun on their backs, imagining squeaks.

At the burrow they did not dump the leaves in a heap. They wove. Olive’s quick paws tucked stems. Dotty held the circle steady with her long body, a living hoop. Red and gold went in, and then the silver, so the wreath caught both sun and the idea of moon. They hung it at the entrance. It sparkled. It invited.

Little squeaks erupted. The Muffins peeked out, noses wiggling. One mouse touched a silver leaf as if it might sing. Another offered, from a tiny paw, the tiniest round muffin, still warm. Olive and Dotty sat in the grass and shared it, crumbs on whiskers, the stream still singing its pebble song.

Ever since then the Muffins’ door wears its leafy hug, and Olive still slides the mossy rocks, and Dotty still freezes for butterflies — only now, when they pass the burrow, the silver leaves wink, as if the stream has learned a second way to shine.
